Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW YORK (CNN)  -- Spiritual leaders of New York's African-American Muslim communities lashed out Friday at a purported al Qaeda message attacking President-elect Barack Obama and, using racist language, comparing him unfavorably to the late Malcolm X. Ayman al-Zawahiri said Obama was the "direct opposite of honorable black Americans" like Malcolm X. The imams called the recorded comments from al Qaeda second-in-command Ayman al-Zawahiri "an insult" from people who have "historically been disconnected from the African-American community generally and Muslim African-Americans in particular." "We find it insulting when anyone speaks for our community instead of giving us the dignity and the honor of speaking for ourselves," they said in a statement read during a news conference at the Malcolm X and Dr. Betty Shabazz Memorial, Educational and Cultural Center. The al Qaeda statement, an 11-minute, 23-second audio message in Arabic with subtitles in English, appeared on the Internet on Wednesday. Its authenticity has not been confirmed. The message said Obama represents the "direct opposite of honorable black Americans" like Malcolm X.  Watch al Qaeda official criticize Obama » . The speaker also said Obama, former and current Secretaries of State Colin Powell and Condoleezza Rice and "your likes" fit Malcolm X's description of "house slaves." An English translation of the message used the term "house Negroes," Malcolm X's term for blacks who were subservient to whites. The term refers to slaves who worked in white masters' houses. Malcolm X said those slaves were docile compared with those who labored in the fields. iReport.com: Should Obama react to comments? Malcolm X, the fiery African-American Muslim activist from the 1950s and 1960s, was an early member and leader of the Nation of Islam. He left that group in 1963 over disillusionment with its then-leader, Elijah Muhammed, but remained a Muslim. After months of death threats, he was assassinated in 1965 by members of the Nation of Islam, who shot him 16 times at close range. The three men who were convicted of the crime have been paroled. On Friday, Imam Al-Hajj Talib 'Abdur-Rashid, recalling Malcolm X's legacy, said that he "stood for human rights and the principle of self defense ... international law. He would have rejected, and we who are Muslim African-Americans leaders reject, acts of political extremism." The Council on American-Islamic Relations also condemned Zawahiri's comments in a statement issued Thursday. "As Muslims and as Americans, we will never let terrorist groups or terror leaders falsely claim to represent us or our faith," the statement said. "We once again repudiate al Qaeda's actions, rhetoric and world view and re-state our condemnation of all forms of terrorism and religious extremism."

NEW YORK (CNN) — On Friday, religious leaders representing New York’s African-American Muslim population strongly denounced an alleged al Qaeda recording that criticized President-elect Barack Obama, used racist terminology and portrayed him as inferior to Malcolm X.

In the message, al Qaeda’s second-ranking leader, Ayman al-Zawahiri, described Obama as the “direct opposite of honorable black Americans” such as Malcolm X.

The imams characterized Zawahiri’s remarks as “an insult” made by individuals who have “historically been disconnected from the African-American community generally and Muslim African-Americans in particular.”

“We find it insulting when anyone speaks for our community instead of giving us the dignity and the honor of speaking for ourselves,” the leaders said in a joint declaration presented at a news conference at the Malcolm X and Dr. Betty Shabazz Memorial, Educational and Cultural Center.

The recording surfaced online Wednesday. Lasting 11 minutes and 23 seconds, it featured Arabic audio accompanied by English subtitles. Its authenticity had not been verified.

In addition to contrasting Obama with Malcolm X, the speaker said Obama, former Secretary of State Colin Powell, current Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice and “your likes” matched Malcolm X’s description of “house slaves.” The English translation rendered the phrase as “house Negroes,” a term Malcolm X used for Black people who were submissive to whites.

The expression originated in slavery and referred to enslaved people who served inside white slaveholders’ homes. Malcolm X contrasted their perceived docility with the behavior of enslaved laborers who worked in the fields.

CNN invited viewers to watch the al Qaeda official’s criticism of Obama, while iReport.com asked whether Obama should respond to the remarks.

Malcolm X was a prominent and forceful African-American Muslim activist during the 1950s and 1960s. He became an early member and leader of the Nation of Islam but broke with the organization in 1963 after becoming disillusioned with its leader at the time, Elijah Muhammed. He continued to practice Islam after leaving.

Following months of threats against his life, Malcolm X was assassinated in 1965. Nation of Islam members shot him 16 times at close range. The three men convicted of killing him were later paroled.

Reflecting on Malcolm X’s legacy Friday, Imam Al-Hajj Talib ’Abdur-Rashid said Malcolm X “stood for human rights and the principle of self defense ... international law.” He added that Malcolm X would have opposed political extremism, just as African-American Muslim leaders do today.

The Council on American-Islamic Relations also rejected Zawahiri’s statements in a declaration released Thursday.

“As Muslims and as Americans, we will never let terrorist groups or terror leaders falsely claim to represent us or our faith,” the organization said. “We once again repudiate al Qaeda’s actions, rhetoric and world view and re-state our condemnation of all forms of terrorism and religious extremism.”

counterfactuals.output:
# New York Black Muslim leaders condemn al-Zawahiri’s attack on Obama

**NEW YORK (CNN)** — African-American Muslim leaders in New York condemned al Qaeda deputy Ayman al-Zawahiri’s racist remarks about President-elect Barack Obama, calling the comments an attempt to divide Black Americans and discredit Obama’s historic election.

In a message released by al Qaeda’s media arm, al-Zawahiri compared Obama unfavorably with civil rights leader Malcolm X and used a racially charged term commonly translated as “house Negro.” He portrayed Malcolm X as an authentic opponent of oppression while accusing Obama, former Secretary of State Colin Powell and Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice of serving the American political system.

New York Muslim leaders rejected both the language and al-Zawahiri’s effort to invoke Malcolm X, who embraced Sunni Islam after leaving the Nation of Islam and making a pilgrimage to Mecca.

They said Malcolm X’s legacy could not be appropriated by an extremist organization responsible for attacks that killed Muslims and non-Muslims around the world.

The leaders also described Obama’s election as a milestone for African-Americans, even as they acknowledged that Muslims may disagree with some of his policies.

Obama became the first African-American elected president of the United States on November 4, 2008. Al-Zawahiri’s message appeared aimed at undermining enthusiasm for that achievement and at portraying the incoming administration as hostile to Muslims.

Muslim American organizations across the country have repeatedly denounced al Qaeda and terrorism committed in the name of Islam. New York’s African-American Muslim community has been particularly outspoken against attempts by foreign extremist groups to exploit the history of racism in the United States.

The controversy also highlighted Malcolm X’s continuing symbolic importance. Born Malcolm Little, he emerged as one of the most influential Black leaders of the 20th century. After his 1964 pilgrimage to Mecca, he spoke increasingly about racial reconciliation and the universality of Islam before his assassination in New York in 1965.

New York Muslim leaders said al-Zawahiri’s rhetoric distorted that legacy, replacing Malcolm X’s political and spiritual evolution with a message of racial hostility.

Obama’s transition team did not immediately respond to the remarks.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the reaction of Black Muslim imams and the Council on American-Islamic Relations to al Qaeda’s audio message calling Obama, Colin Powell, and Condoleezza Rice “house slaves.”
counterfactuals.output:
In November 2008, al-Qaeda deputy Ayman al-Zawahiri released an audio message describing President-elect Barack Obama, former Secretary of State Colin Powell, and Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice as “house slaves” or “house Negroes.” The message used footage and language from Malcolm X to contrast them with supposedly more authentic Black leaders.

The response from prominent Black American Muslim figures was overwhelmingly hostile:

- **Imam Talib Abdur-Rashid**, a Harlem imam and leader in New York’s African-American Muslim community, rejected al-Zawahiri’s attempt to appropriate Malcolm X. He emphasized that Malcolm’s views developed after his pilgrimage to Mecca and argued that al-Qaeda was distorting Malcolm’s legacy for propaganda.
- **Imam Johari Abdul-Malik**, then outreach director at the Dar al-Hijrah Islamic Center in Virginia, characterized the statement as a racist insult and an affront to African-American Muslims. He said political disagreements with Obama, Powell, or Rice did not justify racial degradation.
- Other Black Muslim activists, including **Mahdi Bray** of the Muslim American Society’s Freedom Foundation, described the message as desperate and divisive and stressed that Obama’s election represented an important achievement for African Americans and the country.

The **Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR)** also issued a direct condemnation. CAIR called the rhetoric racist and inflammatory, rejected al-Qaeda’s attempt to exploit America’s racial history, and reiterated that al-Qaeda neither represented Islam nor spoke for American Muslims. CAIR’s response placed the message within a broader effort to prevent extremist organizations from claiming religious legitimacy or injecting themselves into American political and racial debates.

Overall, the reaction was not merely a defense of Obama, Powell, and Rice. Black Muslim imams and CAIR objected to three things in particular: al-Qaeda’s use of anti-Black language, its selective misuse of Malcolm X, and its claim to speak with Islamic authority on behalf of Muslims in the United States.

counterfactuals.output:
**Black Muslim leaders reject al-Zawahiri’s use of Malcolm X to attack Obama**

**WASHINGTON, November 2008** — African-American Muslim leaders have sharply rejected an attempt by al-Qaeda’s second-in-command, Ayman al-Zawahiri, to use the words and image of Malcolm X to discredit President-elect Barack Obama, calling the message a distortion of Malcolm’s legacy and a cynical effort to inflame racial divisions in the United States.

In an Internet recording released shortly after Obama became the first African American elected president, al-Zawahiri described Obama — along with former Secretary of State Colin Powell and Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice — as a “house Negro.” The phrase came from a well-known 1963 speech in which Malcolm X contrasted enslaved people who identified with the interests of their masters with those who resisted them.

The al-Qaeda leader’s message included archival footage of Malcolm and portrayed Obama as a Black figure serving a hostile American system rather than challenging it. Al-Zawahiri also criticized Obama’s support for Israel and his promise to send more U.S. troops to Afghanistan.

But Black Muslim leaders in the United States said the comparison ignored both the meaning of Obama’s election and the development of Malcolm X’s own political and religious thinking.

They argued that Obama had not been installed by a white power structure to pacify African Americans. He had won a national election through a broad coalition that included millions of Black voters, other racial minorities and white Americans. Whatever disagreements Muslims might have with his policies, they said, describing him with language rooted in slavery demeaned African Americans and trivialized their history.

The criticism was especially offensive, several leaders said, because it came from an al-Qaeda official with little connection to the African-American experience. For many Black Muslims, Malcolm X is not a symbol that a foreign extremist movement can simply appropriate. He is part of a distinctly American history of slavery, segregation, religious conversion, self-determination and civil-rights struggle.

Al-Zawahiri’s message relied on Malcolm’s “Message to the Grassroots” speech, delivered while Malcolm was still a minister in the Nation of Islam. In that address, Malcolm used the “house Negro” and “field Negro” metaphor to condemn Black leaders he believed were too closely aligned with white institutions.

African-American Muslims noted, however, that Malcolm’s life did not end with that speech. After leaving the Nation of Islam in 1964, he made the pilgrimage to Mecca, embraced Sunni Islam and began speaking in broader terms about human solidarity. He said his experiences worshipping with Muslims of different races had changed his views about white people and the possibility of overcoming racism.

Malcolm remained an uncompromising critic of racial injustice and American foreign policy until his assassination in 1965. But his later thought, Muslim leaders said, cannot be reduced to a single metaphor from an earlier phase of his career.

That evolution is central to why many believed Malcolm would have recognized Obama’s victory as historically significant, even if he might also have challenged an Obama administration over war, poverty, racism or U.S. policy in the Middle East. Pride in the election, they said, did not require uncritical support for every position Obama held.

The reaction also reflected a wider divide between al-Qaeda and Muslim communities in the United States. African-American Muslims constitute one of the country’s oldest and most established Muslim populations. Their institutions grew out of struggles against racial discrimination and later developed deep ties to mainstream Sunni Islam, neighborhood activism and civic participation.

Most Black Muslim leaders have repeatedly condemned al-Qaeda’s attacks and its claim to speak for Muslims worldwide. They regard voting, community organizing and participation in American public life as legitimate tools for pursuing justice. Al-Zawahiri, by contrast, presents the American political system as inherently illegitimate and has sought to persuade Muslims to withdraw from or attack it.

Obama’s election therefore posed a propaganda problem for al-Qaeda. The sight of a Black man, whose father was a Muslim from Kenya, winning the presidency complicated the group’s depiction of the United States as a society permanently organized around white supremacy. Obama is a Christian and has never identified himself as a Muslim, but his family background and international upbringing also challenged al-Qaeda’s portrayal of America as closed to anyone associated with the Muslim world.

Muslim leaders said al-Zawahiri appeared to be trying to turn those facts against Obama by suggesting that his success proved only that he had submitted to American power. They characterized that argument as an effort to diminish Black political achievement and to discourage Muslims from feeling invested in democratic change.

The attack also revived painful racial terminology. Although English translations rendered al-Zawahiri’s phrase as “house Negro,” some accounts translated it as “house slave.” In either form, African-American leaders said, the expression carried a historical weight that made its use by a non-American militant particularly inflammatory.

There was no consensus among Black Muslims about Obama’s policies. Some were concerned about his positions on Israel, Afghanistan, civil liberties and the broader “war on terror.” Others worried that expectations surrounding the first Black presidency might discourage legitimate criticism.

Yet they distinguished those policy disputes from al-Zawahiri’s racial attack. A person could oppose Obama’s plans, they said, without denying the meaning of his election or branding him a servant of white interests.

For many, al-Zawahiri’s invocation of Malcolm X failed for three main reasons: it froze Malcolm’s legacy at one moment and ignored his later embrace of interracial Muslim fellowship; it treated African-American history as a propaganda device for a foreign militant movement; and it dismissed the political agency of the millions of Black Americans who helped elect Obama.

The strongest rebuttal was therefore not that Malcolm X would necessarily have endorsed Obama’s program. It was that Malcolm’s legacy belongs to a far more complex tradition than al-Qaeda’s message allowed — one that combines resistance to oppression with personal transformation, religious growth and the determination of African Americans to define their own political future.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the controversy surrounding the purported 2008 al Qaeda recording about President-elect Obama, including the response from New York imams, CAIR, and relevant background on Malcolm X.
counterfactuals.output:
In November 2008, shortly after Barack Obama’s election, Islamist websites released a recording attributed to al-Qaeda deputy Ayman al-Zawahiri. Its authenticity was not independently established at first, although U.S. officials and terrorism-monitoring organizations generally treated it as likely genuine.

In the message, Zawahiri attacked Obama over his support for Israel and his plans to continue military operations in Afghanistan. He grouped Obama with Colin Powell and Condoleezza Rice and invoked Malcolm X’s distinction between the submissive “house Negro” and the rebellious “field Negro.” Translations rendered Zawahiri’s Arabic as “house slaves” or “house Negroes,” making the message widely viewed as a racial slur and an attempt to undermine Obama among Black Americans and Muslims.

Muslim leaders in New York, including African-American imams, publicly rejected the recording. They said al-Qaeda had misappropriated Malcolm X, insulted people of African descent, and tried to create divisions between Black Americans, Muslims, and the incoming president. They also emphasized that disagreement with U.S. policy did not justify al-Qaeda’s racism or violence.

The Council on American-Islamic Relations likewise condemned the message as racially inflammatory and extremist. CAIR rejected both the language and al-Qaeda’s effort to exploit legitimate debates over U.S. foreign policy for propaganda purposes.

The Malcolm X reference was controversial partly because it removed his words from their historical setting. Malcolm X used the “house Negro/field Negro” analogy in his 1963 “Message to the Grass Roots” speech to describe different responses to white domination during slavery and in contemporary Black politics. But after leaving the Nation of Islam and making the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1964, he embraced Sunni Islam and spoke more strongly about interracial human solidarity. He remained a forceful critic of racism and imperialism until his assassination in 1965, but New York imams argued that his later development—and his distinctly American struggle for Black liberation—could not fairly be equated with al-Qaeda’s ideology or violence.

**Muslim leaders reject al Qaeda rhetoric at New York press conference**

**NEW YORK (AP) —** Muslim leaders gathered Friday at the Malcolm X and Dr. Betty Shabazz Memorial and Educational Center to denounce al Qaeda’s rhetoric as extremist, insulting and out of touch with the experiences of Black Muslims in the United States.

Speakers said the terrorist organization’s attempts to invoke racial injustice or the legacy of prominent Black Muslim figures distorted a history rooted in community organizing, political engagement and the pursuit of civil rights.

The leaders said al Qaeda did not represent Black American Muslims or the broader Muslim community. They also rejected efforts to exploit grievances over racism, inequality and U.S. foreign policy to justify violence.

Holding the event at the former Audubon Ballroom, where Malcolm X was assassinated in 1965, underscored the speakers’ argument that his legacy should not be appropriated by extremist groups. They described such rhetoric as an affront to Malcolm X, his family and generations of Black Muslims who have worked within American civic life.

Participants also urged news organizations and the public not to treat inflammatory messages from overseas militant groups as reflective of Muslim opinion in the United States.

The Shabazz Center, named for Malcolm X and his wife, Dr. Betty Shabazz, serves as a memorial and educational institution focused on human rights and social justice.
